content.thinking:
I'm planning the design in one careful pass without testing: a red panda rendered in Genshin-style toon shading with gold filigree and a subtle elemental glow mark, sized realistically at about 0.55m body length with a 0.45m tail, balanced on a mossy stone roughly 0.3m tall.

Now I'm working through the skeleton structure—deciding how the stone and panda joints relate. I want to avoid making the stone move when the hips move, so I'm considering a separate root joint positioned at the stone's center with "hips" as a child joint, rather than rigidly attaching the stone to the hips joint itself.

With the hierarchy settled, I'm shaping the mossy stone itself: an icosahedron geometry scaled flat into an oval boulder, with grey stone paint countershaded by moss green on top, positioned so the top sits near y=0.2 and the bottom sinks slightly for grounding.

Thinking about small decorative touches to add character: a gold-trimmed collar with a tassel on the red panda, a tiny glowing cyan-green leaf charm, and a few floating glow motes kept within the bounding volume so nothing extends above it. Considering also a small glowing mushroom accent for extra elemental flavor.

Working through the red panda's anatomy for accuracy — rusty-red coat, darker belly and legs, white facial markings with tear-line stripes, ringed bushy tail, and dark feet — then stylizing it Genshin-style with a slightly larger head and big anime eyes, likely using a warm amber or dendro-green iris color via a decal.

Now I'm planning the pose: four-legged stance on the stone with legs spread for balance and tail arched upward as a counterweight, then working out rough body dimensions in meters — shoulder height, body length, leg proportions — to fit the figure properly on the stone surface.

I'm calculating the stone's ellipsoid dimensions and solving for where each paw contacts the curved surface, computing the foot height at specific x,z offsets so the legs land correctly on the stone's slope.

Now I'm turning to the skeleton structure, placing a root joint near the base and building a spine chain running from the hips up through the body toward the head.

I'm settling on a simpler spine chain of 4 points giving 3 spans named "hips", "spine", "chest", then a short separate neck chain running from the chest end to the head base with just two points, named "neck" and "head" so the tip joint doubles as the head orientation.

Then I'll explicitly define the head joint parented to the neck chain's last joint, aimed toward the snout point, with role "head" — making sure the neck chain's parent is the spine chain's final joint so everything links up correctly before I sweep the body geometry along the spine path.

The head joint then parents off the spine chain's final neck joint, using role "spine" throughout. I'm plotting the body path points from hips through chest to the neck end, with heavier rump radii fitting a red panda's proportions.

Setting fur radii that taper from hips to neck, with a slight belly sag applied via shift offset. For coloring I'm using countershading with a russet back and darker chestnut belly, wrapping the fur edge shader in a cel-paint function for toon-style lighting.

Now I'm layering in fur card tufts for extra richness - russet tips with lighter highlights, scattered across the body, tail, and cheeks to add texture detail beyond the base shading.

Shifting to the head shape: I'm sizing a wide, rounded skull for that red panda look with a short snout, positioning the head joint and aim point to work out the local bone orientation for the head.

Now I'm working out the head coloring scheme for a red panda face: russet crown, white muzzle and cheeks, white eyebrows, and dark tear marks. I need to define a paint function based on each point's position relative to the head's center, using forward/up/lateral offsets to carve out the cheek and muzzle regions.

Adding a dark tear-line marking below the eye and keeping the crown russet-toned. I'm now working out the actual ellipsoid geometry for the head, figuring out radii and the forward offset so I can place the eyes at the correct azimuth and elevation within those local coordinates.

For eye placement I settle on roughly ±30° azimuth and 8° elevation on the skull surface, matching the decal convention where azimuth 90° is the creature's +X side. I want eye size proportioned sensibly against head width, and I need to make sure the muzzle, which sits in front of the skull as a separate part, doesn't overlap or obscure the eyes.

I check the geometry: eyes around 36° azimuth with roughly 0.059 offset give enough clearance from a narrower, ~0.03-radius snout, so the overlap concern resolves. The decal's default orientation uses world up, mirroring across the x-axis for symmetry, and alpha cutout lets the eye ink and blush sit cleanly over the fur base.

I decide to turn off the default brow decal since red pandas have distinctive white brow spots, planning to add those as separate white parts instead. For the snout, I'm placing a scaled sphere forward and slightly below the head joint, positioning the tip near forward 0.205, and setting up a jaw bone pivot point to aim the lower jaw toward that snout tip.

Adding facial details now: a cream capsule for the lower jaw, a small black-plum nose sphere with a tiny white glint at the snout tip, an ink philtrum line, and a dark sweep curve for the closed mouth with corners anchored at the upper edge of the lower jaw.

For the ears, I'm planning large rounded-triangular red panda ears set wide atop the head, upright and tufted white inside with russet outer fur. I'll build each as two extrudes—a larger russet outer shape and a smaller cream inner shape offset forward—using a rounded-triangle outline with smoothed corners, oriented to face slightly forward-outward on each side of the head.

I'm working out the ear's exact placement on the skull, checking it falls properly on the head's ellipsoid surface, and defining the orientation vectors so each ear tilts outward and slightly forward while its extrusion thickness faces front.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry—outer ear with a bevel, and an inner ear layer offset slightly forward along the thickness direction, smaller and cream-colored, computing the local thickness vector for positioning.

Red panda ears have dark outer backs with white front edges, so I'll color the outer russet with cream rim accents on the walls. For cheek fluff, I'm thinking small cream spikes pointing outward/back on each side, maybe three per cheek using bone-based spike helpers, plus considering a cheek sphere for extra volume.

Still working out the spike directions and positions for the cheek tufts...

Now I'm checking the texel density given the baked paint area — around 0.6 m² painted gives roughly 1100 texels/m, so about 1mm resolution, which is fine for a stone-sized creature. Eyes don't need glow. Moving on to the front legs: short, thick limbs with shoulder joints positioned at the sides of the chest.

Working out leg placement against the stone's curved surface, I realize the current stone size causes feet to sink too deep as z increases, so I'm enlarging the stone to roughly 0.68m wide and recomputing foot heights — front and hind feet both land around y=0.21, keeping the stance fairly symmetrical front to back.

Still refining leg geometry...

Checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance against the segment lengths to confirm the fold works out geometrically, then extending the chain forward from the wrist to build the paw geometry.

Now I'm working out the hind leg structure: hip to hock joints with thigh and shank segments, bending forward since red pandas stand plantigrade on their soles rather than digitigrade. I'm naming the hind chain joints and planning the foot geometry extending forward from the ankle to form the sole and toes.

I'm sizing the leg tube radii with a slight taper from thigh to paw, choosing a dark chestnut-black color for the fur, and figuring out where to position the front paw as a scaled ellipsoid at the wrist.

Now I'm working out the vertical placement math so each paw sits correctly on the uneven stone ground, defining wrist and paw-center heights relative to ground contact per foot. I'm also planning small toe bumps and tiny claw cones for each paw—four toes and four claws per foot across all four legs, about 32 small parts total, built through a manual loop.

I'm figuring out how the leg chain's tip joint attaches the foot bone, using the chain's last joint as the bone reference. Then I'm sketching the bushy, ring-patterned tail geometry—thick at the base, curving upward and back from the rump for balance, with a sequence of control points defining its arc.

Now I'm setting up the tail's chain structure (naming segments, varying radii for a bushy taper, raised to about 0.82 height) and considering how to paint alternating ring bands of color along its length.

I'll settle on about 11 rings for the tail, picking a bold russet-orange and a darker brown-red to alternate, aiming for a Genshin-style saturated contrast rather than the subtler real-life red panda coloring.

I need the paint-shading function to properly handle cases where a ring color is passed as a Paint instance versus a plain string, making sure shadows resolve correctly at each point along the tail so the coat texture shades consistently.

For the tail fluff, I'm planning fur tufts and spiky wisps scattered along the tail's silhouette using cards on the sweep surface, leaning outward with a flow direction that follows the tail's actual curve rather than a fixed downward direction, so I need to compute the tangent at each point along the tail path.

I realize coloring the tufts with the paint's ring function won't work since I was reading color at a fixed point with no spatial variation, so instead I should project each texel's position onto the tail path to get a parameter along its length, though I'm wary this closestT calculation could get expensive across many texels during baking.

Given that, I'll simplify by just using two fixed tuft texture variants with slightly different colors, chosen randomly per card, rather than ring-matching. I'm now sketching the tuft SVG shape itself as a flame-like silhouette with a darker base and lighter tip.

Writing SVG path code...

Then for scattering: body cards use the bodySweep with filters on normal direction and size range, leaning backward with the fur flow, totaling around 160 cards. Since red pandas lack a chest bib, I'll skip that and move to the head, planning cheek ruff tufts scattered around the cheek area in cream tones.

Head crown gets a few scattered russet cards rather than a full treatment, and I'm skipping the white belly claw idea since it doesn't apply here. For whiskers, I'm using thin rod strokes sweeping outward from the muzzle in cream and ink tones, a few per side with very fine radius.

Now I'm working out a small gold collar accessory looping around the neck joint, figuring out which joint along the spine corresponds to the neck position so I can wrap a cross-sectional loop at the right spot.

I'm placing the collar higher, nearer the head, using a point partway along the spine chain and sweeping a closed gold band around it with a two-tone cel-shaded gold material. I'm also considering adding a wider teal cloth collar underneath the gold trim for extra visual interest.

For the finishing touch, I'm hanging a charm at the chest front — a gold ring with a glowing teal gem and cream/teal tassel cords — attaching it by casting from the body's centerline outward toward the front-lower chest to find the exact surface point where the neck ring sits.

Building the charm geometry...

Adding tassel cords hanging from the charm...

I'm also thinking about a forehead ornament now: a gold filigree circlet looping around the skull, with a teal gem centered and small tassels dangling by the cheeks, built as a band swept around the head at a slight forward tilt.

Working out the exact height is tricky since it needs to clear the eyes and pass just below the ear bases without overlapping the ears themselves — checking the elevation and radius at that cross-section of the skull to make sure it fits cleanly.

I'm now placing a thin gold circlet with a small front gem, keeping it horizontal and clear of the snout, then working out hanging chain tassels from the sides of the circlet using azimuth/elevation hit points on the skull surface.

For the moss-covered stone with cards, I'm scattering tufts, tiny glowing teal mushrooms, small flowers with gold centers, ferns, grass blades, pebbles, and floating green glow motes to build a lush dendro-style scene.

Scattering moss cards on the stone surface with mottled green tones, then adding small flowers made from stems, petal rings, and gold centers along the stone's edge.

Still working through bone assignment...

Now I'm figuring out the rotation angle so each petal's long axis points radially outward without needing a ring mesh. For mushrooms, I'm planning a dome cap using a partial sphere geometry with a cylinder stem, adding glowing spots on cream-colored caps with a teal tint.

I'm settling on a glowing blue-green mushroom look with flat emissive caps for a soft glow, mint-white dots for texture, and planning small flat-shaded icosahedron pebbles with moss paint plus grass blade cards scattered around the base.

I'll keep the stone's lowest point barely touching the floor, let pebbles sit just above ground level, and add a modest ring of six small floating glow motes near the top without them overlapping the tail height.

For rigging, I'm deciding ear joints should attach to the head at the ear base without needing a special role, while the jaw gets a "jaw" role and the tail chain a "tail" role, keeping legs as named chains with a "leg" role. I'll define left/right sides with simple sign conventions (+X for left) to drive symmetric limb coordinates next.

Now I'm working through the shoulder-to-wrist leg geometry using world coordinates directly, placing the shoulder joint inside the body near x=0.06-0.07, y≈0.39, and the wrist around x=0.085-0.095 lower down. I'm checking that leg tube radius and body radius don't clash awkwardly, estimating leg length at roughly 0.14 units vertically down to the stone surface, and noting the legs read as thick and fluffy which fits a red panda's proportions.

I'm computing elbow bend angles using distance between shoulder and wrist joints versus total limb segment length, getting about a 34° bend which feels natural, then settling on segment lengths near 0.088 each. For the hind leg I'm calculating hip-to-ankle distance accounting for ground curvature at that point, factoring in the terrain height formula to find the actual ankle y-position before finalizing hind leg segment lengths.

Now I'm sizing the hind thigh with a tapered tube radius, then positioning the hind paw forward of the ankle with an elongated scale for the longer hind foot shape and toes extending further forward. I'm mirroring this for the front paw with a shorter scale, then working out toe sphere positions as four small spheres spread symmetrically across the front of each paw.

Adding claws with cone spikes, settling on ivory for the claw tint and dark brown-black for the paw pads, then shifting focus to the overall coat palette -- a bright russet-orange for the back with lighter highlights, and a deep chestnut-black tone for the belly and underside.

Nesting the fur-edge layers works fine since colors can themselves be paints. Now I'm defining the head paint as a position-based function computing distances from the head center to drive the facial shading pattern.

Still writing head paint math...

Working out the white facial region, defining it where the muzzle and cheeks fall below a threshold depth and vertical position, checking it stays consistent with the skull ellipsoid bounds.

I'm also figuring out the cream-colored nose bridge "T" shape and spotting where small white eyebrow decals should sit relative to the eye geometry and ear base, making sure the lifted decals don't clash with other facial features.

Still defining zigzag boundaries...

Still writing color logic...

Placing the nose tip near the snout end, then setting up the lower jaw as a tapered capsule hinged at a joint point, colored to match the cream snout.

I'm figuring out where the snout's lower rim meets the jaw's top surface to place the mouth seam, then sketching a thin ink line for the lip and philtrum running down the front of the snout.

Writing mouth curve points...

Computing forward depths along the mouth curve at various lateral offsets, mapping out surface points where the mouth line sits on the ellipsoid.

I'm reconsidering the geometry though — the lower jaw capsule would actually cover this mouth line, so I need to reposition the mouth closer to the snout's lower rim where the jaw tapers, recalculating the lift and depth values for that lower position.

Then I'm sketching a simple mouth: a philtrum curve plus two short smile curves meeting near the snout sides, accepting a small lift adjustment to avoid the mouth getting buried under the jaw geometry. For the jaw itself, I'm defining a capsule shape running along the snout with tapering radii, placing its tip within the snout profile.

I'm checking that the jaw cylinder's radius leaves the chin visible below the snout bottom, planning a cream chin color and a thin dark ink line where jaw meets snout, and deciding to keep the mouth closed without teeth or fangs for a simpler stylized look.

Now I'm planning gold jewelry accents: bracelet cuffs looping around the foreleg sweep paths with small gems, matching anklets on the hind legs, and a wider gold ring band around the tail.

I'm working out the loop radius parameters for these gold bands, confirming that surface loops only apply to sweep meshes and that the cutting plane needs to align with the tangent at each point to avoid errors.

I'm also considering adding a teal saddle cloth or sash across the back for a color accent, trimmed with gold dashes and a hanging tassel, positioned as a mid-body loop with a painted zigzag pattern along the cloth's width.

Working out the angle math for the gold dash pattern around the body's circumference...

Spacing the chain links about 1.25cm apart. For the tassel, I want it hanging off the band's left side, so I'll place a hit point with the skin wrap angled slightly downward there, then attach a gold bead with a teal strand dropping down along the body toward the belly area.

Now adding a gold ring around the tail, placing it along a horizontal section near the rump so the loop plane follows the tail's tangent and only cuts the tail geometry, not the body. I'm also planning stone surface details -- moss tufts, tiny ferns, a small flower cluster, and a glowing dendro-style rune glyph decal on the front face of the stone, using a textured part that glows in its own texture colors.

Working out the glyph's placement so it sits visible beneath the panda's chin, with the moss painting underneath remaining visible around the decal edges, and sketching the rune design itself as a ring with an inner leaf/sprout symbol and dots in glowing green.

I'll keep it to a single carved glyph plus mushrooms, motes, and the gem rather than adding extra carved sides or veins. For the motes, I'm placing tiny glowing spheres scattered loosely around the stone at varied heights.

I also want a few floating leaves nearby, built from a simple curved outline with a sharp tip, colored flat green with a soft glow—around four of them angled differently. Tallying parts now: the stone, pebbles, moss patches, flowers, leaves, motes, and mushrooms should keep the scene lively without overloading the geometry count.

Then for the panda itself, I'm breaking it into body, tail, four leg sweeps, paws, individual toes and claws, and a detailed head—adding up to roughly 150 parts total, which feels manageable given the triangle counts. For finishing touches, I'll skip lash details but add a small cream tuft inside one ear, plus a tiny gold torus ring as an ear-cuff on just the left ear for asymmetry, with a dangling teal tassel for a playful accent.

I'm working out the torus placement using the ear's local frame direction helper so the cuff orients correctly along the edge tangent, and double-checking how the extrude outline's x/y axes map for the left ear versus the right.

Then I'm adding a dangling tassel from the cuff: a thin gold rod hanging down, a bead, and a teal spike cone forming the tassel tip, positioned so it drapes naturally across the cheek.

Skipping teeth detail for now. Checking that the decal weighting on the skull works correctly against the hit points, and verifying the surface scatter, hit frame, and normal functions all line up properly.

For the body, I'm sweeping along the spine chain with radii keyed evenly over the parameter, using round caps so the hips end smoothly.

Setting up the spine chain with a catmull curve through five control points, parented to root, naming the four joints hips/spine/chest/neck so they match the spline spans exactly with no extra tip segment — root stays the single unparented joint and hips becomes the first spine joint as the docs require.

Now I'm working out joint parenting for the limbs: front legs attach to the chest joint since its z-position falls between chest and the shoulder points, hind legs and the tail both parent off the hips joint.

For the tail I'm plotting six control points starting inside the rump sphere and curving upward and back into a loose S-shape, checking that the bushy tip radius doesn't push the total model height too far past the body, then adding a slight sideways x-offset at each point to break perfect symmetry for a more natural pose.

Settling on a rounded tip with a slightly smaller end radius for the bushy tail, then working out a ring-painting scheme that varies band placement along the tail using a zigzag pattern tied to position and angle.

Adding ragged sawtooth edges that alternate per ring, darkening the very tip, and wrapping the tail's gradient logic in a nested paint function so it correctly resolves the current coordinate state. The ears and spine gradients seem fine as they are, so I'm moving on to finalize the body shading.

For the stone geometry, I'm weighing icosahedron detail levels — higher detail gives a rounder, less rock-like shape, so instead I'll perturb the vertex positions with deterministic noise after generation to get a proper jagged stone look rather than relying on subdivision alone.

Still tuning bump function...

Checking that the sink for feet and bump amplitude stay small enough not to distort the silhouette noticeably, since bumps displace radially by roughly 2-3% of the body scale.

Now I'm computing where the panda's feet land on the ellipsoid surface — using the radii (rx=.34, rz=.36, ry=.13, cy=.115) to find the flat plateau region near the top where it can stand, and confirming the foot height comes out around 0.217 given its (x,z) position. I'm also checking the bottom extent of the body at cy minus ry.

I'm thinking I should just clamp any vertex that sinks too far below the floor back to a flat minimum y, so the bottom stays grounded instead of floating or sinking excessively.

For texture, I'm sketching a paint function that blends moss onto the stone based on surface-facing-up noise, layering light and dark moss near the top and switching to plain stone lower down, plus adding cell-based crack lines using Voronoi distance differences to darken thin seams on the non-mossy areas.

Now I'm thinking about shading the stone with faceted cel lighting, then scattering moss tufts and flattened "pillow" cushions across the upward-facing stone surface while keeping them away from visibility issues under the panda, and finally adding small grass card clusters around the base at ground level attached to the root bone.

I'm then considering whether to add a thin lumpy ground disc of mossy earth beneath the stone to ground the diorama, flattening it enough to stay within the base height tolerance.

Setting frames at y=0.01 with a sink adjustment for the turf grass positioning. Now I'm adding Genshin-style features—ear tufts and eyes—plus whiskers on each side of the snout, computing rod directions from local head coordinates outward.

Mapping out the imports needed for the build: builder, frame, limb/IK, math helpers, path utilities, paint/noise tools, texture and toon-style kits for eyes and fur shading, plus a glow effect—being careful to only import what's actually used since unused imports will throw type errors.

I'm working through the leg construction: computing limb points for hip to foot with bend directions for the knee joint, then building a chain from those points with named segments (thigh, shin, foot) parented appropriately for the leg role.

For the leg sweep radii, I'm using a three-value array so the taper reads naturally through the joint, and I'm picking darker chestnut tones for the fur coloring on the upper versus lower leg to match the red panda's coat pattern.

I'm positioning gold wrist cuffs by sampling the leg chain near the wrist point, using the chain's frame orientation to build a small loop that wraps perpendicular to the limb's tangent at that location.

Now I'm starting the actual export, defining the metadata and color palette constants for the red panda model—russet tones, belly and leg shades, and cream highlights.

Adding more color constants...

Setting up the builder with a root joint, then defining stone placement parameters for an elliptical base shape.

Still shaping the rock geometry... Then I'm adding moss cushion clusters at scattered positions on the stone's surface using small icosahedron lumps.

I'm defining a mottled moss paint texture and figuring out placement angles for small decorative flowers and mushrooms around the stone's edges, checking they stay clear of the panda's feet region.

Writing SVG blade shapes...

Setting up moss and grass card scattering with size, bone, and spin variation, then thinking about mushroom cards next.

Writing mushroom geometry code...

Adding an underside disc to close off the dome's bottom opening so it's not see-through, rotating it to face downward and giving it a cream tone.

Now I need the glow color to be a string rather than a paint object. I'm sketching the flower generator: a stem rod, two small leaf spheres, a loop of five petals, and a tiny glowing gold center sphere, all anchored to the stone surface.

Adding pebble geometry with reused stone paint, then starting an SVG rune decal with concentric circles and a dashed inner ring plus a leaf-shaped path outline.

Working out where the decal should land on the stone surface, checking the hit point's elevation and azimuth so the glyph sits centered on the front slope without clipping, and considering whether the decal's glow needs an emissive map tied to the material.

For the second, smaller rune on the right side, I'll let it inherit its direction from the hit normal automatically rather than specifying one, since the hit already orients to the surface normal — that should keep it legible from the front camera angle.

Now building the head joint, aiming it slightly upward and forward from a head base position, and setting up a local helper function to compute offsets in forward/up/left space relative to the head frame...

Still writing head and skull geometry...

Working out ear joint placement relative to the head joint and skull surface, computing the offset so the ear base sits correctly against the skull curvature before extruding the ear shape.

Still writing ear geometry...

Adjusting the base position slightly lower toward the skull. For ear coloring, I'm picking a dark russet/chocolate tone for the outer ear and a cream tuft for the inner ear, matching red panda reference coloring.

Working out the inner ear tuft outline and extrusion offsets, placing the inner cream shape slightly forward and up from the base so it sits nested within the outer ear with the right thickness and front-facing depth.

Now I'm positioning a gold cuff ring on the left ear, using the ear's local coordinate frame to place it near the base edge, adjusting u,v slightly inward to account for rounding so the torus ring sits properly encircling the ear's rim.

Skipping the stud idea too — I'll try a gold band wrapping around the ear instead, sizing a flat rectangular strip slightly larger than the ear's thickness and width so it encloses the ear edge like a clasp.

Adding a gold gem stud to the front of one ear, then a hanging tassel accessory for the left ear only—a thin gold rod with a bead and a teal spike dangling down, as an asymmetric decorative touch. Considering whether to also add a filigree circlet, though it risks clashing with the ears.

I'm placing the circlet as a horizontal ring slightly above the skull's cross-section, but checking the height carefully since it could collide with the eye tops or the ear bases depending on exact placement.

Settling on a dy of +0.05 for the circlet so the ears appear to emerge through the gold band and the eyes stay clear by a few millimeters, shrinking eye height slightly for safety. Now I'm positioning the central gem using a spherical angle lookup on the skull at roughly 38° elevation on the front.

I'm placing the teal-glowing octahedron gem with a gold setting plate beneath it, then planning symmetric dangling teardrop charms hanging from the circlet near the cheeks, outside the eye azimuth, checked against the eye position to avoid overlap.

The circlet itself gets swept along the closed loop path in gold with a thin radius, using bone weights from the path for deformation.

Now I'm setting up the body as a skin sweep, then building the eyes with anime-style iris coloring and a blush tint, keeping defaults mostly in place aside from the iris hue and disabling brows.

For the eye decals, I'm placing them symmetrically on either side of the head by finding surface hit points at a fixed azimuth and height, mirroring one side, and sizing them small relative to the head. I'm thinking through the decal's facing direction so the drawing reads correctly from the front rather than appearing foreshortened by the surface's curvature, leaning toward a direction vector that's mostly forward with a slight outward component.

Now I'm planning the forehead fur: scattering small tuft cards across the top of the skull filtered by normal direction, using two tuft texture variants (russet and light) in a modest count with small sizes, and considering whether to add cream-colored cheek ruff cards as well.

Then I'm setting up the cheek tufts with a filter based on horizontal distance from center and vertical position, giving them an outward-and-back flow direction and a lean angle, followed by scattering a larger set of body tufts across the torso filtered by upward-facing normals, alternating between the two tuft textures with a steeper lean and slight bend.

Next I'm adding a separate darker belly tuft group filtered for strongly downward-facing normals, then tail tufts swept along the tail's path with a deeper lean and a third darker texture variant, and finally leg tufts near the wrist using a dedicated dark leg-tuft texture.

I'm working out the collar loop placement along the spine — figuring out exactly where t≈0.78 lands in arc-length terms and checking whether that cross-section plane clears the skull's back curvature so the collar sits cleanly below the head without intersecting it.

Now I'm defining the collar itself: a teal cloth sweep with small gold rings offset along the chain, then adding a decorative charm attached at the bottom-front of the collar using a ray-hit on the body surface, with a gold backing disc and a gem shape stuck onto that point.

Writing tassel rigging...

I'm positioning the hanging tassel near the chest and neck area, checking the waist band placement, then starting to compute leg and paw joint positions for each side of the body.

Working out shoulder, wrist, hip, and ankle coordinates for front and hind limbs, deciding on joint naming conventions and chain names, and setting parent joints for the leg chains relative to the spine.

Writing paw geometry function...

Working out front and hind paw positions with these length parameters, checking that the leg angles look reasonable relative to the shoulder and hip joints, then moving on to paw coloring based on the leg paint scheme.

Now I'm placing the toe spheres with slight scale variation and spacing offsets to fan them out across the paw width, positioning claw spikes at each toe tip in ivory, and verifying the gradient blend function properly clamps at the endpoints.

I'm checking joint counts across the skeleton—root, spine, head, jaw, ears, four legs with three joints each, and the tail—confirming they total 27, then sketching the body sweep radii that taper from the rump through the torso with a slight downward shift vector for the belly contour.

Working through the leg and tail proportions now, setting thigh and shoulder mass radii, tapering tail segment widths across six samples, and double-checking that the tail base height matches the rump before moving on to textures and type signatures for the chain and path inputs.

Now I'm scattering pebbles around the ground ring, computing each one's vertical position so its base sits flush with the turf, then starting on the grass card placement with randomized angles.

Checking the turf mound shape and grass card placement against the stone surface to make sure the sink depth and heights line up—lowest point stays around -.012 which is fine, and overall height with tail tip and floating motes stays under 1. Moving on to check stone surface details.

Now I'm drafting the full module: setting up imports for the builder, frame, IK limb helpers, math utilities, paint tools (mottle, gradient, cells, noise), the catmull path helper, SVG texture, glow kit, and toon shading helpers, confirming each one maps to a specific part the model needs—mottle for moss and turf, gradient for legs, cells for cracks, frame for grass. Starting to define the color palette and cel-shaded materials...

I need to make sure HC is defined before the head paint closure references it, so I'll create the head joint first, then compute HC, then build the paint function referencing it—since paint evaluation happens lazily when the part is read/baked, this ordering should work.

Now I'm working out the tear mark geometry on the face: it should trace a line running from near the eye's lower-inner corner down toward the mouth corner, slanting slightly inward as dy decreases, using a zigzag texture for a furry edge and a distance threshold in dx to carve out the mark shape.

I'm also laying out the white facial patches—lower muzzle white, bridge white, and the brow spot—using similar dz/dy/dx distance conditions to define their boundaries.

Now I'm defining the russet coloring for everywhere else, with a lighter russet patch near the crown, before moving on to writing the stone surface paint function with moss and crack-like cell patterns.

Checking the lighting dot product for a flat-topped surface confirms it's properly lit, then I'm estimating the texture density needed given the stone's surface area relative to other body parts.

Now I'm defining paint functions for turf and moss cushion using mottled cel-shading patterns with distinct colors and seeds, then verifying the extrude type signature for outline points needs proper typing to avoid inference errors on literal arrays.

Writing leaf outline geometry...
